summary.text: In Britain's Industrial Revolution, cloth-making moved out of homes and into mills, centred in south Lancashire and the towns on both sides of the Pennines.
Water frames and spinning mules in water-powered mills spun yarn on a larger scale, and cotton became the most important textile.
Steam engines later let factories be built where waterpower was not available, and power looms in weaving sheds mechanised weaving.

facts.label: Centre of industry
facts.value: South Lancashire and the towns on both sides of the Pennines

facts.label: Before the 1760s
facts.value: Textile production was a cottage industry

facts.label: Flying shuttle
facts.value: John Kay, 1733: cloth woven faster and wider

facts.label: Derby silk mill
facts.value: John Lombe's 1717 mill, arguably Britain's first mechanised factory

facts.label: Weaving shed
facts.value: A mill that specialised in weaving fabric

items.prompt: After weavers adopted a faster shuttle, why did they run short of thread?

options.label: Cotton from India stopped arriving in Britain
The new shuttle worked only with silk thread
Neither kind of spinning wheel could produce enough thread for the looms
Spinners left their homes to work in the new weaving sheds

items.explain: The flying shuttle made the loom twice as productive, and neither the simple wheel nor the Saxony wheel could produce enough thread for the looms.

items.prompt: The patent on a key cotton-spinning design ran out in 1783. What followed?

options.label: Many cotton mills were built
Cotton spinning moved back into homes
Wool mills closed all across the country
Steam engines were banned from spinning

items.explain: The end of the patent was rapidly followed by the erection of many cotton mills.

items.prompt: A mill owner wants a site far from any dependable stream. What lets him power his machinery there?

options.label: Larger water frames driven by a bigger wheel
Packhorses carrying thread to a mill by a river
Hand-turned spinning wheels worked in nearby cottages
Steam engines driving his machines instead of a water wheel

items.explain: Steam engines let mills be built where waterpower was not available or not steady through the seasons.

items.prompt: Why was steam power at first a poor fit for spinning?

options.label: It could not produce enough power to turn a single spindle
Its poor speed control caused the thread to break
It worked only in towns that were far from any water
It had been invented after spinning moved into mills

items.explain: Early steam engines had poor speed control, which caused thread breakage, though the engine could pump water over a water wheel to drive the machinery instead.

items.prompt: By the 1820s all the spinning had moved into mills. What was still done at home?

options.label: Spinning, which stayed at the cottage wheel
Carding, done by families around the hearth
Weaving, done by outworkers in their own homes
Dyeing, done in small workshops beside the mill

items.explain: By the 1820s all cotton, wool and worsted was spun in mills, but the yarn went to outworking weavers who worked in their own homes.

items.prompt: A mill finds it has more engine power than its spinning machines need. What does the owner do with the surplus?

options.label: Adds power looms in weaving sheds
Switches back to water frames
Sells the engine to a cottage weaver
Closes the weaving sheds

items.explain: Surplus power capacity encouraged the construction of more sophisticated power looms working in weaving sheds.
